definition: An object that produces a magnetic field and attracts magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time and does not need an external field to maintain it. Made from hard magnetic materials such as steel.
A material that becomes a magnet only when placed in an external magnetic field. Made from soft magnetic materials such as iron. Loses its magnetism when the external field is removed.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic force is experienced. Represented by field lines that go from north to south pole outside the magnet.
A line used to represent a magnetic field. The direction of the line shows the direction of the force on a north pole. Lines are closer together where the field is stronger.
The end of a magnet from which magnetic field lines emerge. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract — a north pole is attracted to a south pole.
The end of a magnet into which magnetic field lines enter. Attracted to a north pole; repelled by another south pole.
The force between unlike magnetic poles (north and south) or between a magnet and a magnetic material, pulling them together.
The force between like magnetic poles (north-north or south-south) pushing them apart.
A material that can be attracted by a magnet. Magnetic materials include iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.
A device containing a small, freely rotating magnet (needle) that aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field, pointing towards magnetic north.
The magnetic field surrounding the Earth, produced by electric currents in the Earth's liquid iron core. It acts like a giant bar magnet with poles near the geographic poles.
The magnetic effect produced by an electric current. When current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire.
A coil of wire that, when carrying an electric current, produces a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet. The field is strongest inside the coil.
A solenoid with an iron core inside it. The iron core becomes an induced magnet, greatly increasing the strength of the magnetic field. The magnetism can be switched on and off.

A rule used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire. Point the thumb in the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers show the direction of the field.
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field. The force is perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.

A rule used to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. The thumb points in the direction of motion (force), the index finger in the direction of the field, and the middle finger in the direction of conventional current.
The force acting on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. Calculated using: F = BIL, where B is magnetic flux density, I is current, and L is length of conductor in the field.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field. Symbol B, measured in tesla (T). A stronger magnetic field has a greater magnetic flux density.
The SI unit of magnetic flux density (T). A field of 1 tesla exerts a force of 1 newton on a 1-metre conductor carrying a current of 1 ampere.
A device that uses the motor effect to convert electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy. A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences forces that cause it to rotate.
A device in a DC electric motor that reverses the direction of the current through the coil every half turn, ensuring the coil continues to rotate in the same direction.
The process by which a changing magnetic field induces (generates) a potential difference (voltage) in a conductor. The basis of generators and transformers.
The voltage generated in a conductor when there is a change in the magnetic field through it or when the conductor moves through a magnetic field.
The induced potential difference is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux. A faster change or stronger field induces a greater potential difference.
The direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change that caused it. This is consistent with the conservation of energy.
A device that converts kinetic energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A coil rotating in a magnetic field generates an alternating current (AC).
An electric current that repeatedly reverses direction. Generated by rotating coils in magnetic fields. The UK mains supply is AC at 50 Hz and 230 V.
An electric current that flows in one direction only. Produced by batteries and solar cells.
A device that uses electromagnetic induction to change the voltage of an alternating current. Consists of two coils (primary and secondary) wound around an iron core.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the supply voltage. The alternating current in this coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core.
The output coil of a transformer. The changing magnetic field from the primary coil induces a potential difference in this coil.
A transformer where the secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, resulting in a higher output voltage than input voltage.
A transformer where the secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary coil, resulting in a lower output voltage than input voltage.
Relates the voltages and number of turns in a transformer: Vp/Vs = np/ns, where Vp and Vs are primary and secondary voltages, and np and ns are the number of turns in each coil.
The network of pylons, cables, and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the country.
Energy lost as heat in the cables of the National Grid due to the resistance of the wires. Calculated using P = I²R. Using high voltage and low current reduces power loss.
